[Diagram: horizontal field lines pointing to the left; a straight wire crosses them at $70^\circ$, running from upper left to lower right, current $3.7\ \mathrm{A}$ with arrow pointing down the wire.] The current through the wire is $3.7\ \mathrm{A}$. What is the force on the wire and the direction in which the force acts? (force / N; direction) A $2.2 \times 10^{-3}$, into the paper B $2.2 \times 10^{-3}$, out of the paper C $5.9 \times 10^{-3}$, into the paper D $5.9 \times 10^{-3}$, out of the paper

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct use of $F = BIl\sin\theta$ plus Fleming's left-hand rule.
questions.misconception: Using $\cos\theta$ instead of $\sin\theta$, or misapplying Fleming's left-hand rule

explanation.body: The force is $F=BIL\sin\theta=(3.4\times10^{-2})(3.7)(0.050)\sin70^\circ=5.9\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{N}$. By Fleming’s left-hand rule, the leftward field and downward current component give a force into the paper.

perOption.A: Uses the component parallel to the field to calculate the force.
perOption.B: Uses the parallel component and reverses the force direction.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Reverses the force direction.

[Diagram: square region of field into the page (crosses); electron enters horizontally from the left and curves downward through a quarter circle, exiting moving downward.] Which statement(s) is/are correct? 1 The force on the electron is $9.6 \times 10^{-16}\ \mathrm{N}$. 2 The gain in energy of the electron is zero. 3 The change in momentum of the electron is zero. A 1 only B 1 and 2 only C 1 and 3 only D 3 only

questions.difficultyReason: One substitution into $F = Bqv$ plus recognising that a magnetic force does no work but changes momentum direction.
questions.misconception: Thinking constant speed means momentum is unchanged

explanation.body: The magnetic force has magnitude $B|q|v=(2.0\times10^{-3})(1.60\times10^{-19})(3.0\times10^6)=9.6\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{N}$. It provides the centripetal force for uniform circular motion, so speed and kinetic energy stay constant. The velocity changes direction, so the momentum changes.

perOption.A: Omits statement 2 even though the kinetic energy stays constant.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Includes statements 1 and 2 only.
perOption.D: Includes the false statement 3 and omits both true statements.

questions.stemText: The diagram shows a beam of electrons entering a velocity selector. The direction of the electric field is as shown in the diagram. Electrons with the desired speed leave the selector undeflected. In which direction is the magnetic field? [Diagram: box with electron beam entering from the left and leaving to the right; electric field arrows drawn in perspective pointing out of the page towards the viewer. Direction options at the exit: A upward, C downward, B into the page (away from viewer), D out of the page (towards viewer, same as E).]

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires 3D visualisation and applying the left-hand rule to negative charges.
questions.misconception: Treating electrons as positive charges when applying the left-hand rule, or setting B parallel/antiparallel to E

explanation.body: The electron is negatively charged, so its electric force points along B. The magnetic force must point along D for the beam to remain undeflected. Fleming's left-hand rule, with conventional current opposite to the electron beam, gives magnetic field direction C.

perOption.A: This field reverses the magnetic force, making it reinforce the electric force.
perOption.B: The magnetic force would be perpendicular to B and could not oppose the electric force along B.
perOption.C: Correct. Field direction C produces a magnetic force along D.
perOption.D: The magnetic force would be perpendicular to D, although the required force is along D.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A rigid square coil of sides 50 mm has 100 turns. It hangs vertically such that it can rotate freely about one side. When a current of 0.40 A passes through the coil, it hangs in equilibrium at an angle of 30° to the vertical with its lowest side in the vertical magnetic field of a magnet. The weight of the coil is 0.30 N. [Diagram: coil seen edge-on, pivoted at top, tilted 30° to the vertical; weight 0.30 N acting downward at its middle; lower side (current shown as a dot/cross symbol) sits between an S pole above and an N pole below.] What is the flux density of the field between the magnets? A 0.038 T B 0.043 T C 0.075 T D 0.087 T

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combines F = BIL with N turns and a principle-of-moments calculation using the correct perpendicular distances.
questions.misconception: Using the wrong perpendicular distances or forgetting that only the bottom side is in the field

explanation.body: The magnetic force $NBIL$ on the lowest side acts horizontally to the right. Balancing moments about the pivot gives $Mg(L/2)\sin 30^\circ=NBIL(L\cos 30^\circ)$. Substituting $0.30(0.025)\sin 30^\circ=100B(0.40)(0.050)(0.050)\cos 30^\circ$ gives $B=0.043\ \mathrm T$.

perOption.A: Omits the $\cos 30^\circ$ factor from the magnetic force's moment arm.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Omits the $\sin 30^\circ$ factor from the weight's moment arm.
perOption.D: Uses the full side length in the weight's moment arm.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: An electron moving in a straight line passes through small holes P and Q in two identical plates. [Diagram: two horizontal plates with holes; the electron path is vertical, upward from Q to P.] There is a uniform electric field $E$ and a uniform magnetic field $B$ between the two plates. The directions of these fields are shown by arrows or these symbols: ⊙ a field coming out of the paper; X a field going into the paper. Which orientation of the two fields is not possible? A $E$ downward, $B$ upward B $E$ into paper, $B$ out of paper C $E$ diagonally down to the right, $B$ into paper D $E$ out of paper, $B$ to the right

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires 3D direction reasoning for both forces on a negative charge across four field combinations.
questions.misconception: Assuming E and B must always be perpendicular for undeflected motion

explanation.body: In B, the magnetic force on the upward-moving electron points left, and the electric force points out of the page. Both forces are transverse to the path and point in perpendicular directions, so they cannot cancel. The resulting transverse force deflects the electron from the straight path.

perOption.A: The magnetic field is parallel to the velocity, so only the electric force acts, accelerating the electron along the path.
perOption.B: Correct. The transverse forces cannot cancel.
perOption.C: The key treats C as possible by balancing lateral forces, but the upward electric force changes the speed and breaks that balance.
perOption.D: The electric force into the page can balance the magnetic force out of the page.

questions.stem:
Two long, straight, current-carrying wires, X and Y, are parallel. The current in wire X is 2 A and the current in wire Y is 5 A.

Which diagram shows the correct combination of the magnitude of the forces and the directions of the current in wires X and Y?

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires two ideas: equal and opposite forces (Newton's third law) and attraction for parallel currents.
questions.misconception: Thinking the wire with larger current exerts or feels a larger force

explanation.body: By Newton's third law, the forces on the two wires have equal magnitudes. Currents in the same direction attract, while currents in opposite directions repel. In A, both currents flow downwards, so each force points towards the other wire.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows unequal forces and repulsion between currents flowing in the same direction.
perOption.C: Shows attraction even though the currents flow in opposite directions and should repel.
perOption.D: Shows unequal forces even though the two forces are a Newton's third-law pair.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A straight, thin conducting wire of mass 50 g and length 0.20 m lies horizontally on a flat surface in a uniform horizontal magnetic field. The magnetic field is directed at an angle of 60° to the wire. When a steady current of 10 A flows through the wire, the normal reaction force exerted by the surface on the wire decreases to half of its original value.

What is the magnetic flux density of the field?
questions.stemText: A straight, thin conducting wire of mass 50 g and length 0.20 m lies horizontally on a flat surface in a uniform horizontal magnetic field. The magnetic field is directed at an angle of 60° to the wire. When a steady current of 10 A flows through the wire, the normal reaction force exerted by the surface on the wire decreases to half of its original value. What is the magnetic flux density of the field? A 0.14 T B 0.25 T C 0.28 T D 0.49 T

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs $F = BIL\sin\theta$ with the right angle, plus the idea that the magnetic force supplies half the weight.
questions.misconception: Using cos θ instead of sin θ, or equating the magnetic force to the full weight

explanation.body: The normal reaction falls to half the weight, so the upward magnetic force must supply the other half for equilibrium. Thus $0.5mg=BIL\sin60^\circ$, giving $B=\frac{0.5(50\times10^{-3})(9.81)}{10(0.20)(0.866)}=0.142\ \mathrm{T}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The upward magnetic force balances half the weight.
perOption.B: Using $\cos60^\circ$ in the force expression gives about $0.25\ \mathrm{T}$.
perOption.C: Using the full weight as the magnetic force gives about $0.28\ \mathrm{T}$.
perOption.D: Using the full weight together with $\cos60^\circ$ gives about $0.49\ \mathrm{T}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: An electron with charge $e$ and mass $m$ is accelerated from rest through a potential difference $V$. It then enters a region containing a uniform electric field of field strength $E$ and a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$. These fields are perpendicular to each other and to the electron's velocity. The electron passes through this region undeflected. Which expression correctly represents the ratio $\dfrac{e}{m}$? A $\dfrac{E}{2VB}$ B $\dfrac{B^2}{2VE^2}$ C $\dfrac{2VE^2}{B^2}$ D $\dfrac{E^2}{2VB^2}$

stemImage.alt: Question 24: An electron with charge e and mass m is accelerated from rest through a potential difference V. It then enters a region containing a uniform electric field of f

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Two standard relations (accelerating p.d. and velocity selector) combined algebraically.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to square v = E/B when substituting into the kinetic energy

explanation.body: Acceleration from rest gives $\tfrac12 mv^2=eV$, so $e/m=v^2/(2V)$. In the velocity selector, the electric and magnetic forces balance, giving $Bev=eE$ and $v=E/B$. Substituting this speed gives $\frac{e}{m}=\frac{E^2}{2VB^2}$.

perOption.A: This substitutes $v$ where the energy equation requires $v^2$.
perOption.B: This inverts the speed ratio $E/B$ before squaring it.
perOption.C: This multiplies by $2V$ when isolating $e/m$, which requires division by $2V$.
perOption.D: Correct. It combines the energy equation with the force balance.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A negatively charged particle is projected into a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly.

Which quantity does the period of its motion not depend on?
questions.stemText: A negatively charged particle is projected into a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly. Which quantity does the period of its motion not depend on? A The mass of the particle. B The charge of the particle. C The magnetic flux density. D The velocity of the particle.

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Standard derivation of the cyclotron period that students often memorise.
questions.misconception: Assuming a faster particle takes less time to complete the circle

explanation.body: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force, so $B|q|v=mv^2/r$. Cancelling $v$ and using $v=2\pi r/T$ gives $B|q|=2\pi m/T$. Therefore $T=2\pi m/(B|q|)$, independent of the particle’s velocity.

perOption.A: The period is directly proportional to the mass.
perOption.B: The period is inversely proportional to the magnitude of the charge.
perOption.C: The period is inversely proportional to the magnetic flux density.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two ions P and Q pass through a velocity selector un-deviated. Ion Q has 2 times the charge and 1.5 times the mass of ion P.

They then enter a region of uniform magnetic field where P travels in a circular arc of radius 3.7 cm.

What is the radius of the circular arc travelled by ion Q in the uniform magnetic field?
questions.stemText: Two ions P and Q pass through a velocity selector un-deviated. Ion Q has 2 times the charge and 1.5 times the mass of ion P. They then enter a region of uniform magnetic field where P travels in a circular arc of radius 3.7 cm. uniform magnetic field velocity selector ions P and Q What is the radius of the circular arc travelled by ion Q in the uniform magnetic field? A 1.2 cm B 2.8 cm C 4.9 cm D 11 cm

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must realise the velocity selector fixes equal speeds, then use r = mv/(qB) as a ratio.
questions.misconception: Assuming the ions have equal kinetic energy or forgetting both mass and charge change

explanation.body: Both ions pass through the velocity selector undeflected, so they have the same speed. In the uniform magnetic field, $Bqv=mv^2/r$, giving $r=mv/(Bq)$. Since $B$ and $v$ are the same for both ions, $r_Q=(3.7)(1.5/2)=2.8\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Divides by both the mass factor and the charge factor.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Inverts the mass-to-charge ratio when scaling the radius.
perOption.D: Multiplies by the charge factor even though radius is inversely proportional to charge.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Two long, straight, current-carrying wires, X and Y are at a perpendicular distance 5.0 m apart. The current in X is 3.0 A and into the plane of the paper, while current in Y of 6.0 A is towards the top of the page. Point P is on the line of shortest distance joining the two wires, at a distance 2.0 m away from wire X as shown. [Diagram: wire X shown end-on with current 3.0 A into the page; wire Y drawn vertically in the plane of the page 5.0 m to the right with 6.0 A upward; P lies on the horizontal line between them, 2.0 m from X.] What is the magnitude of the resultant magnetic flux density at point P? A $3.5\times10^{-12}$ T B $5.0\times10^{-7}$ T C $6.3\times10^{-7}$ T D $7.0\times10^{-7}$ T

stemImage.alt: Question 24: Two long, straight, current-carrying wires, X and Y are at a perpendicular distance 5.0 m apart. The current in X is 3.0 A and into the plane of the paper, whil

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs fields from two wires and recognising the two contributions are perpendicular.
questions.misconception: Adding or subtracting the two fields as if parallel

explanation.body: Using $B=\mu_0 I/(2\pi d)$, wire X gives $3.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T}$ towards the bottom of the page at $d=2.0\ \mathrm{m}$. Wire Y gives $4.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T}$ out of the page at $d=3.0\ \mathrm{m}$. The fields are perpendicular, so $B_{\mathrm{resultant}}=\sqrt{(3.0\times10^{-7})^2+(4.0\times10^{-7})^2}=5.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\varepsilon_0$ in place of $\mu_0$.
perOption.B: Correct. The fields add at right angles.
perOption.C: Swaps the distances from P to wires X and Y.
perOption.D: Adds the field magnitudes directly as if the fields were parallel.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A current-carrying thin wire $30\ \mathrm{cm}$ long with a mass of $2.4\ \mathrm{g}$ is initially suspended at rest above the ground when placed in a uniform magnetic field of flux density $0.040\ \mathrm{T}$.

The wire experiences an upward acceleration of $1.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ when a current $I$ passes through it.

[A horizontal wire above the ground lies in a magnetic field directed into the page, shown by crosses.]

If the current in the wire is $\frac{I}{2}$, what will its acceleration be?

A. $0.60\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, upward
B. $4.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, upward
C. $4.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, downward
D. $5.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, downward

stemImage.alt: Question 24: A current-carrying thin wire 30 cm long with a mass of 2.4 g is initially suspended at rest above the ground when placed in a uniform magnetic field of flux den

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding the initial current and recalculating the signed net force at half that current.
questions.misconception: Halving net force when only magnetic force halves

explanation.body:
Taking upward as positive, $BIL\sin\theta-mg=ma$. Initially, $0.040I(0.30\sin90^\circ)-0.0024(9.81)=0.0024(1.2)$, giving $I=2.202\ \mathrm{A}$.

At half the current, $0.040(1.101)(0.30\sin90^\circ)-0.0024(9.81)=0.0024a$. Thus $a=-4.305\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, or $4.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ downward.

perOption.A: Halves the original acceleration even though weight stays the same.
perOption.B: Reverses the direction of the net force, which points downward once weight exceeds magnetic force.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the magnetic force per unit mass as the magnitude of the net acceleration.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two infinitely long straight conductors X and Y are placed parallel to each other. Each conductor carries a current I in opposite directions to each other. Point P is equidistant from either conductor. The magnetic flux density at P due to each conductor is B.

X is fixed while Y is rotated about the axis ZZ’ until it is perpendicular to X and its current is into the plane of the paper.

What is the final resultant magnetic flux density at P in terms of B?
questions.stemText: Two infinitely long straight conductors X and Y are placed parallel to each other. Each conductor carries a current I in opposite directions to each other. Point P is equidistant from either conductor. The magnetic flux density at P due to each conductor is B. X is fixed while Y is rotated about the axis ZZ’ until it is perpendicular to X and its current is into the plane of the paper. X Y I I d d Z Z’ P What is the final resultant magnetic flux density at P in terms of B? A 0 B B  C 2 B D 2B

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires visualizing the rotated wire and adding two perpendicular field vectors.
questions.misconception: Adding field magnitudes without checking directions

explanation.body: After Y is rotated, its field at P points upward and has magnitude $B_Y=\mu_0 I/(2\pi d)=B$. The field from X points out of the page and has magnitude $B_X=\mu_0 I/(2\pi d)=B$. The fields are perpendicular, so the resultant magnitude is $\sqrt{B^2+B^2}=\sqrt{2}\,B$.

perOption.A: Treats the fields as opposite and cancelling.
perOption.B: Counts only one conductor's field.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Adds magnitudes as if the fields pointed in the same direction.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The diagram shows two long, straight, parallel wires, separated by a distance $d$. Wires P and Q carry currents of $\mathrm{4.0\ A}$ and $\mathrm{3.0\ A}$, respectively, in the directions shown.

[Two vertical wires intersect the horizontal dashed line OX. P is on the left with an upward current arrow and Q is on the right with a downward current arrow. The horizontal separation is labelled $d$.]

At a point on the line OX, the resultant magnetic flux density due to the currents in the two wires is zero.

What is the distance of this point from P?

Option | distance from P | position
A | $\frac37 d$ | between the wires
B | $\frac47 d$ | between the wires.
C | $4d$ | to the left of P
D | $4d$ | to the right of Q

stemImage.alt: Question 23: The diagram shows two long, straight, parallel wires, separated by a distance d. Wires P and Q carry currents of 4.0 A and 3.0 A, respectively, in the direction

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Determine which side permits cancellation and use the two different distances in the field equation.
questions.misconception: Equating field magnitudes where both fields point the same way

explanation.body: The currents run in opposite directions, so the fields point the same way between the wires and can only cancel outside. The cancellation point must be nearer the smaller current, so it lies to the right of Q. If its distance from P is $y$, its distance from Q is $y-d$. Equating the two field magnitudes gives $4.0/y=3.0/(y-d)$, so $y=4d$.

perOption.A: Between the wires the fields point the same way, so they add at this position.
perOption.B: This balances field magnitudes between the wires, where the fields reinforce each other.
perOption.C: To the left of P, P has both the larger current and the shorter distance, so its field is stronger.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Four particles independently move at the same speed in a direction perpendicularly to the same magnetic field.

Which particle is deflected the most?
questions.stemText: Four particles independently move at the same speed in a direction perpendicularly to the same magnetic field. Which particle is deflected the most? A A proton B An electron C A copper ion D A helium nucleus

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Compare the curvature of particle paths using the mass-to-charge ratio.
questions.misconception: Comparing charge alone to predict deflection

explanation.body: For perpendicular motion, the magnetic force supplies the centripetal force, giving $r=mv/(|q|B)$. With the same $v$ and $B$ for all four particles, the electron has the smallest mass-to-charge-magnitude ratio and therefore the smallest radius and greatest deflection.

perOption.A: A proton has the same charge magnitude as an electron but a much larger mass.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: A copper ion has a much greater mass per unit charge magnitude than an electron.
perOption.D: A helium nucleus carries twice the electron’s charge magnitude but has a much greater mass per unit charge magnitude.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Three long parallel straight wires, X, Y and Z, are equally separated and placed in the same plane. They carry a current of I, 2I and 4I respectively.

If the force per unit length between wire X and wire Y is F, what is the force per unit length acting on wire Z?
questions.stemText: Three long parallel straight wires, X, Y and Z, are equally separated and placed in the same plane. They carry a current of I, 2I and 4I respectively. If the force per unit length between wire X and wire Y is F, what is the force per unit length acting on wire Z? A 0 B F C 2F D 3F

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The two current products, separations and force directions must all be compared.
questions.misconception: Ignoring force direction or wire separation

explanation.body: For a long straight wire, $B=\mu_0 I/(2\pi r)$, so for the adjacent wires X and Y the force per unit length $F$ is proportional to $2I^2/r$. On Z, X gives an attractive force per unit length proportional to $4I^2/(2r)$, equal to $F$, and Y gives a repulsive one proportional to $8I^2/r$, equal to $4F$. These act in opposite directions, so the resultant is $4F-F=3F$.

perOption.A: Assumes the opposing forces have equal magnitudes.
perOption.B: Counts only the attraction towards X.
perOption.C: Treats X and Z as adjacent, giving an attraction of $2F$ instead of $F$.
perOption.D: Correct.

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must find each force direction and resolve the symmetric forces into components.
questions.misconception: Magnetic force magnitudes on bent segments add directly.

explanation.body: Each segment experiences a force of magnitude $BIL$. Fleming’s left-hand rule gives upward components for both forces and horizontal components that cancel. Each upward component is $BIL\sin30^\circ$, so the resultant is $2BIL\sin30^\circ=BIL$ towards the top of the page.

perOption.A: Reverses the force direction given by the current and inward field.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Adds the full force magnitudes and reverses the resultant direction.
perOption.D: Adds the full magnitudes instead of their upward components.

An electron enters perpendicularly into a shaded region of uniform magnetic field directed out of paper.

Which of the options shows a possible path of the electron?

[The electron enters the shaded rectangular region moving horizontally to the right. Path A curves downward, B goes straight diagonally downward, C goes straight horizontally and D curves upward. The region is labelled “uniform magnetic field out of the paper”.]

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must reverse the electron’s direction to apply Fleming’s left-hand rule.
questions.misconception: Treating electron motion as conventional current.

explanation.body: The electron moves right, so the equivalent conventional current points left. With the field out of the paper, Fleming’s left-hand rule gives an upward force at entry. The force stays perpendicular to the motion, producing an upward-curving circular path.

perOption.A: Curves downward as a positive charge would.
perOption.B: Shows a straight deflection even though the magnetic force continuously changes the direction of motion.
perOption.C: Assumes zero force even though the electron moves perpendicular to the field.
perOption.D: Correct. The electron initially curves upward.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An experiment is conducted to determine the magnetic flux density of a pair of magnets using a current balance.

A square wire frame, of negligible mass, is supported horizontally on a knife edge so that XY of the frame lies perpendicular to a pair of magnets of length $L$. Current $I$ flows in the wire frame, while a mass $m$ is hung at a distance $q$ from the knife edge. The wire frame is in equilibrium when XY is at distance $p$ from the knife edge.

[Side XY runs between two magnets over length $L$. The knife edge crosses the square frame parallel to XY. The mass $m$ hangs from the opposite side. The distances from XY to the knife edge and from the knife edge to the opposite side are $p$ and $q$, respectively. Current $I$ points right along the rear side and left along the front side.]

Which expression gives the magnetic flux density $B$ between the magnets?

A $\frac{mgq}{I(p+q)p}$
B $\frac{mq}{I(p+q)p}$
C $\frac{mgq}{ILp}$
D $\frac{mq}{ILp}$

stemImage.alt: Question 25: An experiment is conducted to determine the magnetic flux density of a pair of magnets using a current balance. A square wire frame, of negligible mass, is supp

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation combines magnetic force on a wire with the principle of moments.
questions.misconception: Using the full side length as the length in the field.

explanation.body: Take moments about the knife edge. At equilibrium the moment of the weight balances that of the magnetic force, so $(mg)q=(BIL)p$. Rearranging gives $B=\frac{mgq}{ILp}$.

perOption.A: Uses the whole side length $p+q$ as the length of wire in the field.
perOption.B: Uses the full side length $p+q$ and substitutes mass for weight.
perOption.C: Correct. The weight and magnetic force produce equal opposing moments.
perOption.D: Omits $g$ when converting the hanging mass to weight.

The magnetic force acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.24 m from the pivot. A hanging mass 0.015 kg, placed 0.32 m from the pivot, balances the wire when the switch is turned on and the current is 1.5 A.

A section of wire of length 0.18 m lies perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field produced by a magnet. When a current flows in the wire, a magnetic force due to the magnetic field acts on it. 0.24 m 0.32 m The magnetic force acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.24 m from the pivot. A hanging mass 0.015 kg, placed 0.32 m from the pivot, balances the wire when the switch is turned on and the current is 1.5 A. What is the magnetic flux density produced by the magnet? A 0.18 T B 0.48 T C 0.73 T D 0.95 T

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combine the magnetic-force equation with torque balance using the correct moment arms.
questions.misconception: Confusing the length of wire in the field with a moment arm.

explanation.body: The magnetic force contributes a moment $BIL(0.240)$ and the hanging mass contributes an opposing moment $mg(0.320)$. By the principle of moments, these are equal. Therefore $B=\frac{(0.0150)(9.81)(0.320)}{(1.50)(0.180)(0.240)}=0.727\ \mathrm{T}$, or $0.73\ \mathrm{T}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the magnetic moment required to balance the hanging mass.
perOption.B: Uses a magnetic moment too small to balance the mass at its $0.32\ \mathrm{m}$ lever arm.
perOption.C: Correct. The opposing moments balance at this flux density.
perOption.D: Overestimates the required magnetic force by assigning too large a moment to the hanging mass.

When the current is first switched on and before the coil moves, which statement is correct?
questions.stemText: A rectangular coil ABCD is mounted on a vertical axle. Its plane is parallel to the field lines of a uniform horizontal magnetic field. Current flows upwards through side DA and downwards through side BC. When the current is first switched on and before the coil moves, which statement is correct? A There is no magnetic force on sides AB and CD. B There is no magnetic force on sides BC and DA. C Sides BC and DA experience forces in the same direction. D All four sides experience magnetic forces of equal magnitude.

options.label: A
options.text: There is no magnetic force on sides AB and CD.

options.label: B
options.text: There is no magnetic force on sides BC and DA.

options.label: C
options.text: Sides BC and DA experience forces in the same direction.

options.label: D
options.text: All four sides experience magnetic forces of equal magnitude.

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Identify the current–field angle for each side and use the opposite current directions on the vertical sides.
questions.misconception: Assuming every segment of a current loop experiences a magnetic force.

explanation.body: The magnetic force has magnitude $F=BIL\sin\theta$. The currents along AB and CD are parallel or antiparallel to the field, so the force on each is zero. BC and DA are perpendicular to the field and carry opposite currents, so their magnetic forces point in opposite directions.

perOption.A: Correct. The field is aligned with AB and CD.
perOption.B: BC and DA are perpendicular to the field, so both experience a force.
perOption.C: Opposite current directions give opposite force directions in the same field.
perOption.D: AB and CD experience zero force, while BC and DA experience nonzero forces.

questions.difficultyReason: The student must resolve the magnetic force relative to the vertical wire.
questions.misconception: Assuming the magnetic force acts along the line separating the wires.

explanation.body: The vertical wire produces a magnetic field into the page on its right. The current in the horizontal wire flows right, so the magnetic force on it acts upwards. It therefore has no component towards the vertical wire.

perOption.A: Parallel currents in the same direction attract.
perOption.B: The slanted wire's upward current component produces a force towards the vertical wire.
perOption.C: Correct. The force on the horizontal wire acts upwards.
perOption.D: The antiparallel currents produce a repulsive force.
